title: Modern Warfare 4 Review: Call of Duty Is Back
htmlContent:
A Globe-Trotting Campaign Built on Spectacle

Every year, Call of Duty fans swing between declaring the franchise dead and celebrating its comeback. Modern Warfare 4 lands firmly in the second camp. As the finale of the rebooted trilogy that began in 2019, it delivers confident, big-budget spectacle, even if not every part of the package hits the same high.

The story campaign is the standout. It juggles two threads at once: a North Korean invasion of South Korea and a chase for a powerful MacGuffin led by Captain Price and what remains of Task Force 141. Missions rotate between perspectives, putting players in the boots of South Korean troops, the legendary Price, and even North Korea's leader.

The pacing rarely lets up, and the presentation is outstanding, with top-tier visuals, punchy audio, and lavish CGI cutscenes. A John Wick-style nightclub firefight is a clear highlight.

The one stumble is a sprawling, open-ended mission that doubles as a DMZ tutorial and stalls the momentum. Still, the campaign is loud, ridiculous, and enormously entertaining.

Multiplayer: Solid, Familiar, and Little Else

Multiplayer is the series' cornerstone, yet here it is the weakest pillar, though not because it plays poorly. Grounded but quick movement is a welcome change from the omnimovement of the last two Black Ops games, weapons have heft, and the time-to-kill is fast without being instant.

Domination and Gun Game remain a blast, and the new Gunfight variant stitches together pieces of different maps each round. Matches are short and respawns instant.

The problem is a lack of ambition. Maps are forgettable, and the experience feels nearly identical to what the series has offered since 2019. The usual hooks are here, from attachment unlocks to prestige ranks, but anyone hoping for real evolution will be disappointed.

DMZ Steals the Show

The most interesting addition is the reworked DMZ, the extraction mode that debuted in 2022's Modern Warfare 2. Squads of three drop into a large map filled with points of interest, taking on quests, scavenging materials, and fighting both AI enemies and rival players.

It is slower and more tactical, with fortified zones, roaming bosses, and limited supplies demanding care. Because AI and human opponents are hard to tell apart, every encounter feels tense, though losing a full backpack to an ambush stings.

Successful runs return to the Forward Operating Base, a hub reminiscent of WWII's Headquarters, where players take missions, customize weapons, and manage three characters with deep skill trees. Characters lost on a failed extraction can be bought back at rising costs.

DMZ is impressively big, yet it borrows from so many extraction shooters, Warzone included, that it never masters one idea or matches genre leaders' tension. Instead, it is an accessible, casual extraction experience many will enjoy.

Technical Performance

On both PS5 and PS5 Pro, Modern Warfare 4 holds a steady 60 frames per second while looking superb. DualSense support is excellent as well, with finely tuned haptics that add real impact during the campaign.

Verdict

Modern Warfare 4 is not flawless, but it is a cohesive package. A thrilling campaign and an unexpectedly deep DMZ make up for a multiplayer mode that rarely ventures beyond the familiar. The cycle may turn again next year, but for now, Call of Duty is back.

  • Pros
  • Explosive blockbuster campaign
  • Stunning visuals
  • Immersive DualSense haptics
  • Deep, rewarding DMZ progression
  • Satisfying gunplay
  • Cons
  • Multiplayer offers little that is new
  • Open-ended campaign level disrupts pacing
  • DMZ lacks the tension of top extraction shooters

Score: 7/10 – Good
excerpt: Modern Warfare 4 closes out the rebooted trilogy with a thrilling campaign, a surprisingly deep reworked DMZ extraction mode, and solid if familiar multiplayer, delivering a cohesive package that earns a 7/10 and signals the franchise's return to form.
